results.summary: This design implements a nibble-serial version of the LED block cipher, which encrypts a 64-bit plaintext block using a 128-bit key. Data is loaded and unloaded serially through the 8 input and 8 output pins, with control signals for loading key and plaintext, starting encryption, and reading ciphertext. The design is intended to be controlled by external hardware such as a Raspberry Pi, and test vectors are provided for verification. Notable features include a compact implementation that reuses datapath logic across nibbles, at the cost of higher latency (2045 cycles for encryption).

This design simply turns on one output pin, as described in its minimal documentation. It has no inputs and only eight output pins, all labeled A[0] through A[7]. The testing instructions state that no action is needed, and no external hardware is required. The project appears to be a basic template or test design with essentially no functionality beyond driving an output high.

This project implements a leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron model in Verilog. It accepts an 8-bit input current on ui_in and outputs an 8-bit state variable on uo_out, with a spike signal on uio[7]. The documentation is very sparse, providing only a brief description and no detailed testing procedure or external hardware requirements. It is presented as a tutorial, but the lack of documentation makes it difficult to assess its completeness or correctness.

This design is a 16-bit floating-point multiplier that uses logarithmic approximation to reduce hardware complexity and power consumption. It has 8 input pins for operand A, 8 bidirectional pins for operand B, and 8 output pins for the product, with the pins time-multiplexed to handle 16-bit values. The documentation is minimal, consisting only of a one-line description and pin names, with no detailed explanation of the algorithm or testing procedure. Notable aspects include the use of approximation for efficiency, but without further documentation, its accuracy and limitations are unclear.

This project implements a VGA-based binary clock that displays hours, minutes, and seconds in binary format on a VGA monitor. It uses a Chisel-generated design with inputs for selecting the time source (internal or external 1 Hz or 32.768 kHz), buttons for setting the time, and switches for selecting display modes. The design outputs VGA signals (red, green, blue, hsync, vsync) and debug signals on the bidirectional pins. External hardware includes a VGA PMOD, buttons, switches, and optionally a real-time clock for precise timekeeping.

This design is a 4x4 structural array multiplier that takes two 4-bit unsigned inputs and produces an 8-bit product. It uses full adders to sum partial products, as described in the documentation. The design is intended to be tested with a testbench of varying input values, and no external hardware is required. It is a straightforward educational example of a digital multiplier.

This is an SPI test design based on the tt07_alu_74181 project, as stated in the documentation. It includes SPI signals (MISO, MOSI, clock, chip select) and inputs for CPOL and CPHA, but the documentation provides no further details on functionality or testing. The design is likely a template or test for SPI communication, but its exact behavior is unclear from the available information. No external hardware is required according to the description.

This project implements a synchronous FIFO with a 4-bit data width. It has inputs for write and read control, 4-bit data input, and outputs for full, empty, and 4-bit data output. The documentation mentions that it is based on a debouncing mechanism, but the testing procedure is listed as 'TBA' and no external hardware is required. The design is a basic first-in-first-out memory buffer.

This project implements a Tamagotchi-like artificial creature called Mimosa, which reacts to external stimuli such as tickling, playing, talking, feeding, and temperature changes. It outputs emotional states like sleeping, eating, playing, smiling, babbling, kicking legs, doing nothing, and crying, and includes SPI and UART interfaces for debugging. The design is supported by extensive simulation, FPGA prototyping, and a microcontroller-based logger for debugging. Notable aspects include its complex behavioral model inspired by biological processes and its use of multiple subprojects for testing and emulation.

This project implements a mixed-precision leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron that can compute either one neuron with a 24-bit membrane value and 8-bit weights or two neurons with 12-bit membrane values and 4-bit weights. It has 4 input pins for weights, a ready output, and two spike outputs for upper and lower neurons. The documentation is minimal, with testing instructions stating to apply weights and observe spikes, and no external hardware is required. The design is notable for its mixed-precision approach, but further details are lacking.
